articles.text: Later reports state the loss by the burning of the Miles City Dressed Beef Co's slaughter-house at $40,000, on which there was no insurance. The butchers passed through Medora last week on their way to Chicago and report that the intention of rebuilding, has been abondoned. The firm intends now to either hire or rent a building in Chicago and ship cattle there alive. They have about 5,000 contracted for that they will dispose of in this way.
articles.summary: The Miles City Dressed Beef Co. slaughter-house fire loss is put at $40,000, uninsured; the firm will not rebuild and will ship cattle alive to Chicago.

articles.text: Word comes from T. R. Selmes that those who have not already done so, should immediately send certified checks to the Frst Nat. Bank of Mandan, for the amount taxed against them by Stark county. This is not in payment of the tax, but is to be held in trust by the bank, until the suit is decided. It is understood that any other person or firm taxed by Stark county whether residing in Billings county or not, can thus send in a certified check and escape taxation unless the case is decided against us. The above plan is simply another way of putting up a bond for costs. It is undoubtedly a fairer plan, as each then assumes the full measure of his own responsibility, instead of putting it on the shoulders of bondsmen. Our case looks as promising as ever and we see no reason why we should not win. We learn that there are still a few tax-payers who have not joined in the agreement to fight the case, but will be equally benefited in the decision. This is doubtless owing to the fact that they do not realize that this case involves the right of taxation by Stark county, of all outsiders assessed by it and consequently all are interested who come under this head. All who have not yet done so should express a willingness to stand their share of the expense.
articles.summary: T. R. Selmes asks taxpayers resisting Stark county's taxation to send certified checks to the First National Bank of Mandan, held in trust pending the suit.

articles.text: To the average reader, it must seem absolutely impossibe that the soldiers who are after the Apaches in Arizona, can be brave men. We have continually seen articles in eastern papers, drawing unfavorable comment from the fact that a thousand soldiers have for more than a year been chasing a hundred Apaches and have virtually accomplished nothing. When we think that the Bad Lands are almost a level prairie in comparison with he country in which the Apaches are fighting, that they know every inch of it, that they are as well or better armed than the soldiers, that they can on foot run clear away from a troop of cavalry in a day, that they leave almost no trail, that they are constantly subdividing into bands of from three to twenty and striking where they are least expected, that they can live in luxury where soldiers would starve and that man for man there is no body of troops in the world a match for them on their chosen battle ground, the results of the campaign are more easily explained. About the only feasible way now seems to be to furnish a sufficient number of troops so that every water hole could be guarded and the Apaches kept moving so that exhaustion would finally compel them to surrender.
articles.summary: Editorial defending the soldiers pursuing the Apaches in Arizona and suggesting every water hole be guarded until the Apaches are exhausted.

articles.text: As shown by our report, the cattle market about holds its own, with no particular increase or decrease. There does not seem, however, to be that shaky feeling which characterized last year's market at this season. Prices bid fair to hold up well and there will probably be no long depression. It can be set down as a maxim that good cattle will always bring good figures. Poor cattle will only by accident bring a good price. For instance, Monday, some Colorado and Nebraska grass cattle averaging 1,200 to 1,300 lbs., brought $4.75@$5.00. On the other hand some big, horsey, raw-boned Washington Territory cattle weighing 1,200 lbs., brought only $2.50. Texas cattle are generally very poor and averaging the different grades, did not bring over $2.65. Very few Montana and Dakota cattle have been shipped, but they have brought good prices.
articles.summary: Comment that the cattle market is holding steady and that good cattle bring good prices.

articles.text: Bill Lundy of the 13 outfit, has left the country with no enviable reputation behind him. He has for some time been worming himself into the confidence of other boys in the outfit and borrowing what he could of them. He also drew his pay in advance from the 13 company. Some time ago, he drew more money on the plea of paying some bills in Belfield and started for there. He landed in Medora and with a plausible tale, induced T. W. Gordon to trust him for a suit of clothes. He then boarded the cars and the last heard of him was at Miles City. He came here from the Judith Basin and it is supposed he returned there. The boys of the 13 outfit are especially angered over the actions of this dead beat and want him shown up in all the cow papers of the west. It is just this kind of a rascal that hurts the reputation of cowboys as a class and each should feel it his duty to bring him to justice. Range papers will confer a favor by copying the above.
articles.summary: Bill Lundy of the 13 outfit skipped the country after borrowing from fellow hands, drawing pay in advance and getting a suit on credit from T. W. Gordon in Medora.

articles.headline: Mingusvile Correspondence.
articles.text:
Mingusville July 8th 1886.

Editor Cow Boy.

A terrible wind storm accompanied by rain and hail visited this place yesterday afternoon doing great damage to crops. The water raised five feet in Beaver creek. It also washed out a bridge fifteen miles west of here and delayed No. 1 about eleven hours at Mingusville.

It is rumored that one of Mingusville's cattle men is about to round up one of Glendive's fairest about the 12th. We all give him our best wishes.

The newest thing in Mingusville is that new pool table of Powers & Gidley that they just received from the east.

Mrs. Peter Gallager from Glendive, spent the 4th with us.

The people of this place enjoyed themselves on the 5th at a picnic in the grove near the ranch of S. E. Grindall and report a pleasant time. The evening was spent in dancing and merry making.

Feed is very short in this vicinity but we hope this late rain will improve it.

There are some parties here who think seriously of starting a dog ranch, they have a stock of four now on hand.
articles.summary: Mingusville letter of July 8: a wind, rain and hail storm, a washed-out railroad bridge, a rumored wedding, a new pool table, a July 5 picnic and short feed.

articles.headline: The Longevity of Alfalfa.
articles.text:
The American Agriculturist recently had an article on alfalfa in Colorado in which the writer said the plant was first seeded eight years ago. To our certain knowledge, Major Jacob Downing had alfalfa sowed in his door yard as early as 1863, and the next year L. K. Perrin sowed five pounds of California seed in his field. The seed was furnished by Mr. Perrin's brother, who had made a great success of it in the Sacramento valley. As far back as 1872—fourteen years ago—the colonists of Greely were sowing alfalfa, and some of the original meadows still produce fine stands of it.

In this connection it may be said that alfalfa will hold its growth in ordinary soil for at least a period of forty years—in fact no man of our acquaintance has ever tried it long enough to tell exactly how many years it will remain in perennial rotation.

The writer once interviewed an old native ranchero on his hacienda in the state of Chihuahua, Mexico. The old don had a grand vega of hardy alfalfa on the second bottom, and the writer was informed that it had been growing there for fifty-two years. The plant was healthy and vigorous, and had been subject to cutting every six weeks of its growth. This trip to Mexico was two years ago, and we suppose the stand is still growing, as it showed no signs of decay. It may last seventy-five, a hundred or two hundred years for all we may know of its probable longevity.

It pretty much depends, we may conclude, that the age of alfalfa depends largely on the condition of the under soil. This must neither be too wet, least it rots the lower roots, nor too dry else it will not obtain healthy root and die a "borning." The low river bottoms are not the place for alfalfa, as the rot is very apt to take it off after a year or two of struggle. The extreme high places are generally too sterile for successfull propagation—so then we have solution: We must plant on the intermediate lands, watch it closely in season and out of season until it gets well in root, when it will take care of itself, and forever yield forage in great abundance.

When we wish to learn of alfalfa, or any other Colorado product for that matter, we do not want to look in an eastern agricultural paper for reliable information. In fact the Colorado farmer should have no use for the eastern agricultural papers—they are "no wano" for the west.—[Field and Farm.
articles.summary: Reprint from Field and Farm on how long alfalfa stands last in Colorado and Mexico.

articles.headline: The Reason Why.
articles.text:
In Camp, San Miguel county, N. M. June 26, 1886.—For the past few weeks I have been working, part of my time, in a field that brought me in contact with a number of parties who have been negotiating with capitalists east for the sale of ranch properties, and having seen the correspondence in relation to the same, I am convinced that the cattle business has had a heavy setback, owing to the way many new companies have been run for some time past. All investors seem to write in the same discouraging manner, which is the result of many parties having invested in the business and as yet received no returns from their investments, except in the way of a detailed report from the secretary and treasurer, with vouchers attached. This is an undisputed fact in the case of many cattle companies, and more particularly with those largely composed of foreign capitalists.

Having noticed a good number of old cattle men perfectly contented with their business, I have been more than solicitous to find out the true cause of such a state of affairs, and the most practical illustration that I know of, was given in the following conversation had this week with one of New Mexico's oldest stockmen. I have gone over the above ground pretty thorougly with said stockman, and asking his theory as to the cause of so much dissatisfaction among those who have of late years invested in the cattle business, he replied by telling an experience which he had recently gone through with the company of which he is now manager.

He stated that some years ago he started with a small bunch of cattle, and after a number of years of hard work and close application to his business, he sold his herd to a company composed of eastern capitalists, at a fair market price, and "counted out" at the time of delivery, some 18,000 head of stock cattle. He hired himself to the said company at a good salary as their manager. Things went along nicely for a season or two; they sold some beeves during the time, but not near enough to pay expenses and an interest on the capital invested; stockholders and directors meetings were held, and a general dissatisfaction arose; so one day said manager was forwarded a telegram requesting him to report at once to the headquarters office, and a committee which was authorized by the directors, met him with the interrogatory, why was it that the business did not pay them so well as it had him in the past? To which he replied by saying: "Gentlemen, you have officers of your company, and you pay them salaries of, (per year.)

President at a salary of....................$5,000.00
Secretary and treasurer at a salary of 2,500.00
Bookkeeper and cashier " .. 1,200.00
Manager (and manager only in name) at a salary of.......... 2,500.00
Range foreman at a salary of........... 1,200.00
Trail boss at a salary of.................. 1,000.00

"You also have bought fine thoroughbred bulls, paying as high as $1,000 for one or two, and then any number of grades at from $50 per head up to $100; you have built good camp houses, barns and stables; you buy the best of flour, canned goods, and a quantity of other "Delmonico eatables," with everything else in like proportion, whereas I was my own president, secretary and treasurer, bookkeeper and cashier, manager, range foreman, trail boss, and besides making a d—d good $50 hand myself. Instead of fine camp houses, I lived in "dug-outs," which I made during my spare moments; made ropes out of the hides of dead animals; instead of a "chuck-wagon" filled with fancy eatables, I used a packhorse, carrying a little corn meal and bacon; for branding irons I used bent wire; for bulls I kept trading with my neighbors, and everything else I did in a like manner. Now, if you will do away with a great deal of this unnecessary help and expense, curtail your expenses right and left, or let me be manager in fact, instead of only in name, I will promise to report to you all as often as you desire, and will take for my work or salary, twenty-five per cent, of the profits, after paying all expenses and ten per cent per annum on the capital invested in your company.

The above tells its own story, and without further comment, save that it is like unto [an?] old rubber shoe, it can be made to fit a great many feet at the present day.—[Col. Kansas City L. S. Indicator.

Ranchero.
articles.summary: Reprinted letter from New Mexico blaming over-staffed, extravagant eastern-owned cattle companies for poor returns.

articles.text: The oldest citizen is at last cornered. In all his Dakota experience there is nothing like the continued hot weather of the last three weeks. In all this time there has not been a day that the thermometer has not stood over 110 degress in the sun and once it climbed over the 136 degree fence and smiled cooly at sweltering humanity. Dakota is not alone in its experience however. From all quarters of the United States come wails for relief from a universal spread of the torrid zone. As a practical illustration of the heat, we would state that during the summers of '83 and '84 there was not a night when a blanket was not needed on one's bed. During '85 there was but one night when a blanket was not needed. For the last three weeks, however, a person who was cold blooded enough to need a blanket, might consort with toads and other reptiles.
articles.summary: Three weeks of record heat: never under 110 degrees in the sun, once over 136.
